title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth. A binary tree's maximum depth is the number of nodes along the longest path from the root node down to the farthest leaf node.

examples.explanation: The longest root-to-leaf path has 3 nodes.
The longest root-to-leaf path is 1 -> 2, which has 2 nodes.

hints: The depth of a tree is 1 plus the deeper of its two subtrees.
What is the depth of an empty tree?

title: Invert Binary Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree, invert the tree, and return its root. Inverting means every node's left and right children swap places.

examples.explanation: Every node's left and right children are swapped.
The children of the root trade places.

hints: Inverting a tree means every node's left and right children trade places.
Try it recursively: invert both subtrees, then swap them.
The base case is a null node - there is nothing to invert.

title: Symmetric Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree, check whether it is a mirror of itself (i.e., symmetric around its center).

examples.explanation: The tree is a mirror image of itself.
The right subtree is not a mirror of the left subtree.

hints: A tree is symmetric when its left subtree mirrors its right subtree.
Compare two nodes at a time: one's left child against the other's right child.
Both nodes being null at the same time is a good sign.

title: Same Tree
description: Given the roots of two binary trees p and q, write a function to check if they are the same or not. Two binary trees are considered the same if they are structurally identical, and the nodes have the same value.

examples.explanation: Both trees have the same structure and values.
The structures differ: in p, 2 is a left child; in q, 2 is a right child.
The values at matching positions differ.

constraints: 0 <= number of nodes in each tree <= 10^4
hints: Check the roots first, then recurse on both pairs of children.
Two empty trees are the same; one empty and one not are different.
Values at matching positions must be equal, not just the shapes.

title: Path Sum
description: Given the root of a binary tree and an integer targetSum, return true if the tree has a root-to-leaf path such that adding up all the values along the path equals targetSum. A leaf is a node with no children.

examples.explanation: The path 5 -> 4 -> 11 -> 2 sums to 22.
No root-to-leaf path sums to 5.
An empty tree has no root-to-leaf path.

hints: Subtract the current node's value from the remaining target as you go down.
A valid path must end at a leaf, not just any node.
An empty tree has no path at all.

title: Balanced Binary Tree
description: Given a binary tree, determine if it is height-balanced. A height-balanced binary tree is defined as a binary tree in which the depth of the two subtrees of every node never differs by more than 1.

examples.explanation: Every node's subtrees differ in depth by at most 1.
Node 1's left subtree has depth 3 while its right subtree has depth 1, a difference of 2.
An empty tree is balanced.

hints: A tree is balanced if both subtrees are balanced and their heights differ by at most 1.
You can compute the height and check balance in the same traversal.
If a subtree is already unbalanced, there is no need to keep measuring it.

title: Minimum Depth of Binary Tree
description: Given a binary tree, find its minimum depth. The minimum depth is the number of nodes along the shortest path from the root node down to the nearest leaf node. Note: a leaf is a node with no children.

examples.explanation: The shortest root-to-leaf path is 3 -> 9, which has 2 nodes.
The tree is a skewed chain, so the only leaf is at depth 5.

hints: BFS finds the shallowest leaf naturally, since it explores level by level.
Careful with recursion: a missing child is not a leaf path.
If one child is missing, the answer comes from the other child only.

title: Sum of Left Leaves
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the sum of all left leaves. A leaf is a node with no children. A left leaf is a leaf that is the left child of another node.

examples.explanation: The left leaves are 9 and 15, and 9 + 15 = 24.
A single root node is not a left leaf.
The only left leaf is 4.

hints: Only count a leaf when it is a left child of its parent.
Pass down whether the current node is a left child as you recurse.
The root itself can never be a left leaf.

title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the level order traversal of its nodes' values. (i.e., from left to right, level by level).

examples.explanation: Nodes are grouped by their depth, left to right.
An empty tree has no levels.

hints: Process the tree one level at a time using a queue.
The number of nodes currently in the queue tells you where a level ends.
An empty tree gives an empty list of levels.

title: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the zigzag level order traversal of its nodes' values. (i.e., from left to right, then right to left for the next level and alternate between).

examples.explanation: Level 0 goes left to right, level 1 goes right to left, level 2 goes left to right again.
A single level has no direction to alternate.

hints: It is just level order with the direction flipped on alternate levels.
You can reverse each level's list after collecting it.
Track a boolean flag that toggles after every level.

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree, determine if it is a valid binary search tree (BST). A valid BST is defined as follows: the left subtree of a node contains only nodes with keys strictly less than the node's key; the right subtree of a node contains only nodes with keys strictly greater than the node's key; both the left and right subtrees must also be binary search trees.

examples.explanation: Every node satisfies the BST property.
Node 3 is in the right subtree of 5 but is smaller than 5, violating the BST property.
Node 3 is in the right subtree of 4 but is smaller than 4.

hints: An inorder traversal of a valid BST yields strictly increasing values.
Pass down the allowed (min, max) range for each node as you recurse.
A node's value must satisfy the constraints of ALL its ancestors, not just its parent.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree and two integers p and q, where p and q are the VALUES of two nodes that are guaranteed to exist in the tree, return the VALUE of their lowest common ancestor (LCA). The lowest common ancestor is the deepest node that is an ancestor of both p and q. A node is considered an ancestor of itself.

examples.explanation: Node 3 is the deepest node that is an ancestor of both 5 and 1.
Node 5 is an ancestor of 4, and it is the deepest such node.
Both 7 and 4 are in the subtree of node 2.

constraints: p and q are values of nodes that exist in the tree
hints: If p and q are found in different subtrees of a node, that node is their LCA.
If both are in the same subtree, the answer lies deeper in that subtree.
When the current node's value equals p or q, it is the answer.

title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
description: Given the root of a binary search tree, and an integer k, return the kth smallest value (1-indexed) of all the values of the nodes in the tree.

examples.explanation: 1 is the smallest value in the tree.
The inorder traversal is [1, 2, 3, 4], whose 3rd element is 3.
The inorder traversal is [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], whose 3rd element is 3.

hints: An inorder traversal of a BST visits values in ascending order.
You don't need to store the whole traversal - count as you go.
Stop the traversal as soon as you reach the kth node.

title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
description: Given two integer arrays preorder and inorder where preorder is the preorder traversal of a binary tree and inorder is the inorder traversal of the same tree, construct and return the binary tree. All values are unique.

examples.explanation: The tree is rebuilt level by level in the serialized output.
A single node in both traversals.

constraints: All values in both arrays are unique
hints: The first element of preorder is always the root of the (sub)tree.
Find that root in inorder to split the left and right subtrees.
A hash map from value to inorder index makes the split O(1).

title: Binary Tree Right Side View
description: Given the root of a binary tree, imagine yourself standing on the right side of it, return the values of the nodes you can see ordered from top to bottom.

examples.explanation: From the right side, the visible nodes are 1 (top), 3 (middle), and 4 (bottom).
Each level contributes its rightmost node.
An empty tree has no visible nodes.

hints: The rightmost node at each level is what you see from the right side.
A level-order traversal visits levels one at a time - take the last node of each.
DFS works too if you visit the right subtree before the left.

title: Diameter of Binary Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the length of the diameter of the tree. The diameter of a binary tree is the length of the longest path between any two nodes in a tree. This path may or may not pass through the root. The length of a path between two nodes is represented by the number of edges between them.

examples.explanation: The longest path is 4 -> 2 -> 1 -> 3 (or 5 -> 2 -> 1 -> 3), which has 3 edges.
The only path between the two nodes has 1 edge.

hints: The diameter passing through a node is its left height plus its right height.
The answer is the maximum of that value over every node.
Compute heights bottom-up so each node is visited once.

title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
description: A path in a binary tree is a sequence of nodes where each pair of adjacent nodes in the sequence has an edge connecting them. A node can only appear in the sequence at most once. Note that the path does not need to pass through the root. The path sum of a path is the sum of the node's values in the path. Given the root of a binary tree, return the maximum path sum of any non-empty path.

examples.explanation: The optimal path is 2 -> 1 -> 3 with a sum of 2 + 1 + 3 = 6.
The optimal path is 15 -> 20 -> 7 with a sum of 15 + 20 + 7 = 42.
A path must be non-empty, so the answer is the single node -3.

hints: The best path through a node is the node plus the best downward paths from each side.
A downward path can be empty (contributing 0) if everything below is negative.
Track a global maximum while returning the best single-side path upward.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of Deepest Leaves
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the lowest common ancestor of its deepest leaves. Recall that: the node of a binary tree is a leaf if and only if it has no children; the depth of the root of the tree is 0, and if the depth of a node is d, the depth of each of its children is d+1; the lowest common ancestor of a set S of nodes is the node A with the largest depth such that every node in S is in the subtree with root A. Return the answer serialized in level order.

examples.explanation: The deepest leaves are 7 and 4, and their lowest common ancestor is node 2, returned as its subtree.
The only leaf is the root itself.
Node 2 is the single deepest leaf, so it is its own ancestor.

hints: The answer is the deepest node whose subtree contains all deepest leaves.
Compare the depths of the left and right subtrees at each node.
If both sides reach the same max depth, the current node is the answer.

title: Binary Tree Cameras
description: You are given the root of a binary tree. We install cameras on the tree nodes where each camera at a node can monitor its parent, itself, and its immediate children. Calculate the minimum number of cameras needed to monitor all nodes of the tree.

examples.explanation: One camera on the root's left child covers all four nodes.
A single camera on the root covers the only node.
Cameras on the two middle nodes cover all five nodes.

hints: Think bottom-up: a leaf's parent is the best place for a camera.
Each node ends up in one of three states: needs a camera, has one, or is covered.
A camera covers its parent, itself, and its children - decide greedily from the leaves up.

title: Vertical Order Traversal of a Binary Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree, calculate the vertical order traversal of the binary tree. For each node at position (row, col), its left and right children will be at positions (row + 1, col - 1) and (row + 1, col + 1) respectively. The root of the tree is at (0, 0). The vertical order traversal of a binary tree is a list of top-to-bottom orderings for each column index starting from the leftmost column and ending on the rightmost column. There may be multiple nodes in the same row and same column - in such a case, sort these nodes by their values. Return the vertical order traversal of the binary tree.

examples.explanation: Each column's nodes are listed from top to bottom.
Nodes 5 and 6 share a column; 5 is above 6, so it comes first.
The two nodes with value 2 share column 0 and row 2, so they are ordered by value (they tie, and the order is stable).

hints: Track each node's (row, column) with a BFS from the root.
Group nodes by column, then sort by row, then by value.
The root sits at column 0; a left child goes to column - 1.
